PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child &#38 Family Services Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

Proposition 1 has two major components related to providing mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment to people and addressing homelessness.

# Behavioral Health Transformation (Proposition 1)
With the support of Governor Gavin Newsom, Senator Susan Talamantes Eggman proposed Senate Bill 326 to amend the Mental Health Services Act (MHSA) and Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin proposed Assembly Bill 531 to establish the Behavioral Health Infrastructure Bond Act (BHIBA), also known as the Behavioral Health Bond.
Together, these two bills created the language for the ballot initiative referred to as Proposition 1.
In March of 2024, Californians voted to pass Proposition 1 to modernize the behavioral health delivery system.
The passage of the proposition replaced the Mental Health Services Act of 2004 with the Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) and established the Behavioral Health Bond.

##### Authorizes $6.38 Billion in Bonds to Build Mental Health Treatment Facilities for Those With Mental Health and Substance Use Challenges; Provides Housing for the Homeless. Legislative Statute.
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Counties would need to change some of the mental health care and drug or alcohol treatment services provided currently to focus more on housing and personalized support services.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child &#38 Family Services Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

# Behavioral Health Transformation (Proposition 1)
With the support of Governor Gavin Newsom, Senator Susan Talamantes Eggman proposed Senate Bill 326 to amend the Mental Health Services Act (MHSA) and Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin proposed Assembly Bill 531 to establish the Behavioral Health Infrastructure Bond Act (BHIBA), also known as the Behavioral Health Bond.
Together, these two bills created the language for the ballot initiative referred to as Proposition 1.
In March of 2024, Californians voted to pass Proposition 1 to modernize the behavioral health delivery system.
The passage of the proposition replaced the Mental Health Services Act of 2004 with the Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) and established the Behavioral Health Bond.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child &#38 Family Services Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

# Should California Borrow $8.4 Billion for Immunology Research?
## What to Know About Prop. 1 and Prop. 37, the Other Megabonds
The end is near in our bond measure journey.
Here’s the quick and dirty run-down:
Voting yes on Prop.
1 would mean California could borrow $11.25 billion for all kinds of affordable housing programs, from rentals to student dormitories, to veteran and farmworker housing.

### Background
***Home Loan Program for Veterans.*** The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes.
Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan.
The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
### Proposal
***New General Obligation Bond for Housing.*** Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes.

These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

***Home Loan Program for Veterans.*** The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes.

# Proposition 1
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Home Loan Program for Veterans.*** The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan.
Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes.
Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan.
The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
### Proposal
***New General Obligation Bond for Housing.*** Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes.
This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans.

Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

## Proposition 1: Affordable housing bond
The state would borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing programs, mainly to provide below-market rentals for poor people.
Students and farmworkers also would benefit minimally.
So would military veterans through the CalVet program.
The proposal is packed with goodies aimed at drawing broad political support.
Which it has.
But it’s an expensive item — costing the state at least $500 million annually for 25 years.
Taxpayers already are paying about $6 billion annually to retire $80 billion in bond debt.
This measure is too costly given our fragile, chaotic state budget.
There should have been more prioritizing.
**I’m a “no” vote.**
...

- The article opposes Proposition 1, arguing that although its $11.25-billion housing bond would support important programs, the estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual repayments over 25 years would add too much debt to an already strained budget.

General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs.

Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

1. Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/la-me-all-california-propositions-last-minute-voter-guide
# Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
## Proposition 1
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford.
It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
### Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
...
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income.
...
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans.
Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
...
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments.
They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership.
Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.

Oct. 26, 2026 3 AM PT

- ### Voter guide to the 2026 California general election
Oct. 1, 2026
## Proposition 1: Affordable housing bond
The state would borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing programs, mainly to provide below-market rentals for poor people.
Students and farmworkers also would benefit minimally.
So would military veterans through the CalVet program.
The proposal is packed with goodies aimed at drawing broad political support.
Which it has.
But it’s an expensive item — costing the state at least $500 million annually for 25 years.
Taxpayers already are paying about $6 billion annually to retire $80 billion in bond debt.
This measure is too costly given our fragile, chaotic state budget.
There should have been more prioritizing.
**I’m a “no” vote.**
...
#### Ideas expressed in the piece
- The article opposes Proposition 1, arguing that although its $11.25-billion housing bond would support important programs, the estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual repayments over 25 years would add too much debt to an already strained budget.
...
#### Different views on the topic
- Supporters of Proposition 1 argue that the bond would expand affordable housing and homeownership opportunities for veterans, lower- and middle-income families, and other Californians; the official voter guide cites housing and community-service organizations among its backers.^[10]^

3. Students can't wait for affordable housing. Proposition 1 can help build it.
https://dailybruin.com/2026/11/02/students-cant-wait-for-affordable-housing-proposition-1-can-help-build-it
Proposition 1 will make historic investments in the right solution.
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 would fund the construction of affordable homes, expand homeownership and help our neighbors – all without a single new tax.
This proposition will invest a total of $11.25 billion in housing across California, including $350 million dedicated to affordable student housing at the UC and California State University.
The funding is projected to make higher education more affordable for roughly 40,000 students over the next 50 years.
...
Prop.
1 would create and preserve affordable homes for the people most at risk of losing theirs.
For those already experiencing homelessness, it funds supportive housing that pairs a stable home with the services people need to get back on their feet – the proven way to move people off the streets for good.
Prop.
1 does all of this without raising taxes.
The proposition would unlock federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars that Californians already send to Washington back to build more affordable housing.
And every dollar comes with strict financial accountability measures, including public reporting.
Voters will be able to see exactly where homes are built, how much they cost and how many are constructed.
Join veterans, seniors, teachers, affordable housing advocates and more in voting Yes on Proposition 1 to build the homes California needs, honor veterans who served and give every Californian the opportunity to succeed.

# Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing

It’s called Proposition 1, or the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
...

The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income.
...
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize what I've learned:

**Proposition 1 (November 2026 California ballot): Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026**
- Placed on ballot by Legislature via SB 417, signed by Gov. Newsom
- $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds:
  - $10 billion for housing programs (repaid by General Fund at $500-600M/year for ~25 years, ~0.25% of General Fund)
  - $1.25 billion for CalVet veterans home loans (repaid by veterans themselves; program has never cost the state)
- Allocation:
  - $7.2B multifamily rental housing (up to 40,000 units, 55-year affordability covenants)
  - $1.1B homeownership programs (help ~40,000 households incl. ~2,100 veterans)
  - $500M infrastructure
  - $450M farmworker housing (~2,500 units)
  - $350M student housing UC/CSU (~1,200 beds)
  - $200M tribal housing
  - $200M local pilot programs
  - $1.25B veterans home loans

**Arguments FOR:**
- Nearly 40,000 affordable units designed/permitted/stalled for lack of financing (Enterprise Community Partners)
- State housing bond funds are depleted (2018 bond's $4B was fully committed within 5 years)
- Every state dollar leverages ~$4 from federal/local/private sources; unlocks federal matching funds (LIHTC)
- Housing affordability is the top issue in California; 180,000+ homeless residents
- Cost is modest (~0.25% of General Fund)
- Units remain affordable for 55 years; ~500,000 households could benefit over that period through turnover
